subtitle: The transposition tool that opens new musical worlds. Capos change your guitar's key instantly while maintaining familiar chord shapes and creating unique voicings.

introduction.title: What is a Capo?
introduction.text:
A capo (short for capotasto, Italian for "head of the fretboard") is a clamp that presses down every string at a chosen fret, effectively shortening the guitar's scale length. Because every open string is raised by the same interval, all your familiar open-position chord shapes still work, they just sound higher. A guitarist who only knows a handful of open-position shapes can use a capo to play in any of the twelve keys without learning a single new fingering. That's the whole appeal: the capo trades finger-independence for pitch, letting you keep the easy shapes while the instrument does the transposing.

The device shows up constantly in folk, country, and singer-songwriter music for a very practical reason: it lets a guitarist match whatever key best suits a singer's voice without relearning the song's chords in barre form. It's also a compositional tool in its own right. Moving the capo changes not just the pitch but the tone and feel of the chords, since the strings above the capo are shorter and under different tension, giving the same shapes a brighter, tighter voice than they'd have in open position lower down the neck.

columns.title: How Capos Work
columns.text: Clamping across all six strings at a given fret shortens the vibrating length of every string equally, so each open string rises by one semitone per fret. The relative distances between strings don't change, which is why your existing chord shapes transfer cleanly, but the shorter string length behind the capo does increase string tension slightly and changes the guitar's feel and tone.

columns.title: Musical Benefits
columns.text: A capo lets you transpose a song to whatever key suits a vocalist, without abandoning easy open chords for barre shapes further up the neck. It also opens up voicings you can't otherwise reach: the same G-shape chord played with a capo on the 5th fret rings differently, and often brighter, than the same pitches played as a barre chord in first position.

cards.title: Spring-Loaded Capos
cards.description: Spring-loaded capos clamp shut the moment you squeeze the arms, which makes them the fastest option for changing position mid-set. That speed comes from a fixed spring tension rather than an adjustable one, so the same capo has to work reasonably well on a Telecaster's flat 9.5-inch radius and a classical guitar's much rounder neck, which is where they occasionally fall short. On a guitar they fit well, they're reliable and nearly foolproof; on one they don't, you'll hear buzzing on the outer strings or notice the whole chord pulled sharp.

fields.label: Pros
fields.value: Fast and convenient, reliable clamping, good for live performance

fields.label: Cons
fields.value: May apply too much pressure, can cause tuning issues, less fine control

fields.label: Popular Models
fields.value: Kyser Quick-Change, Dunlop Trigger, Planet Waves NS (micro-adjustment feature)

cards.title: Screw-On Capos
cards.description: A screw-on capo trades the one-handed speed of a spring clamp for a thumbscrew you can dial in to exactly the pressure a given neck needs, which is why session players and touring professionals tend to prefer them. Because you can back off the tension until it's just enough to fret the strings cleanly, these capos are far less likely to pull the guitar sharp, and they hold their intonation across radically different neck profiles. The cost is that adjusting one takes both hands and a few seconds, which matters if you're changing capo position between songs on stage.

fields.label: Advantages
fields.value: Perfect pressure for each guitar, minimal tuning disruption, works on various neck widths, professional studio standard, excellent intonation

fields.label: Top Recommendations
fields.value: Shubb C1 (gold standard), G7th Performance 3 (modern design), Paige Clik (vintage-style professional)

cards.title: Strap-On & Elastic Capos
cards.description: The elastic strap-and-bar design is the oldest style still in common use, and it's still the default on many classical and flamenco guitars because it applies broad, even pressure across a wide neck without a bulky mechanism. It's inexpensive, packs flat, and works as a serviceable emergency capo on almost any instrument, but the elastic loses tension over time and can leave you retensioning it mid-session, which is why gigging steel-string players usually move on to a spring or screw capo once budget allows.

fields.label: Traditional Design
fields.value: Adjustable tension via position, can work on different neck sizes

fields.label: Modern Applications
fields.value: Budget-friendly choice, good for beginners, emergency backup, works on various instruments, lightweight and portable

cards.title: Partial & Specialty Capos
cards.description: Partial capos only clamp some of the strings rather than all six, which means the open strings you leave uncovered still ring at their original pitch alongside the raised ones. That single difference turns the capo from a transposition shortcut into a tuning tool: you can manufacture drone strings and open-tuning-like voicings on a guitar that's still in standard tuning, which is why they show up mostly in the hands of composer-guitarists rather than beginners. Rolling capos solve a different problem entirely, letting a performer slide the capo to a new fret mid-song via a small wheel mechanism, which matters for arrangements that shift key partway through and can't wait for a stop to re-clamp.

fields.label: Partial Capos
fields.value: Capo only some strings (not all six). Create unique open tunings. Advanced compositional tool requiring musical theory knowledge. Used by creative songwriters.

fields.label: Rolling Capos
fields.value: Quick position changes mid-song. Wheel mechanism for fast movement. Professional performance tool. Expensive but efficient. Used by touring musicians.

sections.title: Capo Positions & Key Changes
sections.subtitle: Each fret raises every open chord by one semitone. Use this table to work out what an open-position shape will actually sound like once the capo goes on.
tableRows: G -> A, C -> D, D -> E
G -> Bb, C -> Eb, D -> F
G -> B, C -> E, D -> F#
G -> C, C -> F, D -> G

cards.title: Proper Placement
cards.description: Most tuning and buzzing complaints about capos come down to placement, not the capo itself. Sit it just behind the fret wire rather than on top of it, keep it parallel to the fret rather than angled across the neck, and check every string for buzz before you start playing, since a single loose string will throw off everything you fret above it.
items: Position just behind the fret wire (not on top)
Ensure even pressure across all strings
Check that no strings buzz or mute
Avoid excessive pressure to prevent sharp tuning

cards.title: Musical Applications
cards.description: Beyond the basic key change, a capo is a shortcut to sounds that would otherwise take real technical work. It lets you match a singer's range without relearning a song in barre form, reach voicings that only exist in open position, and simplify chord progressions that would normally demand awkward stretches further up the neck.
items: Play in difficult keys with easy shapes
Enable drop tunings in standard tuning

cards.title: Folk & Country Masters
cards.description: Folk and country guitarists popularized the capo as a working tool rather than a novelty. James Taylor keeps a capo close at hand specifically to sit songs in a comfortable vocal range, while Joni Mitchell went further and combined capo placement with dozens of alternate tunings to build the harmonically dense voicings her writing is known for.

fields.label: James Taylor
fields.value: Frequent capo use for vocal range matching

fields.label: Keith Richards
fields.value: Open G tuning with capo on 5th fret

fields.label: Johnny Cash
fields.value: Simple capo use for key changes

cards.title: Modern Artists
cards.description: The capo remains just as central in contemporary songwriting. Ed Sheeran builds entire loop-pedal arrangements around capoed open chords so that layered parts stay harmonically simple to play live, while John Mayer uses careful capo placement to land on chord voicings that would be far less playable, or would ring differently, without it.

fields.label: Ed Sheeran
fields.value: Extensive capo use for loop pedal arrangements

fields.label: John Mayer
fields.value: Strategic capo placement for unique voicings

fields.label: Mumford & Sons
fields.value: Folk revival with creative capo techniques

cards.title: For Beginners ($10-20)
cards.description: A spring-loaded capo is the right starting point for most new players: it's cheap, forgiving, and needs no adjustment technique to use correctly. At this price point, a reliable clamp matters more than fine-tuned pressure control, since you're still learning what a well-placed capo should feel and sound like in the first place.

cards.title: For Performers ($20-40)
cards.description: Once you're playing out regularly, the small tuning drift a basic spring capo introduces becomes worth fixing. Capos with adjustable pressure hold intonation far more reliably across a full set, which is why most working guitarists eventually upgrade to one even if it costs a bit more up front.

cards.title: For Advanced Players ($40+)
cards.description: Specialty capos solve specific problems rather than replacing your everyday one. A partial capo opens up open-tuning-style voicings without retuning the guitar, and serious players often end up owning two or three different capos for different songs and instruments rather than one do-everything model.

cards.title: Regular Cleaning
cards.description: Clean the rubber padding and metal surfaces regularly. Remove string residue and check for wear on the padding that contacts the strings.

cards.title: Mechanism Maintenance
cards.description: For screw-on capos, occasionally lubricate the threading. Check spring-loaded mechanisms for proper tension and clean pivot points.

cards.title: Storage Tips
cards.description: Store capos in a dry place. Many guitarists keep capos on the headstock for quick access, but avoid leaving them clamped for extended periods.

cards.title: When to Replace
cards.description: Replace capos when padding becomes too compressed, springs lose tension, or adjustment mechanisms become unreliable.
